    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-declarative-contract-tests-and-schema-fencing-2026.json",
    "title": "ADR: Declarative Contract Tests and Schema Fencing",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"ADR: Declarative Contract Tests and Schema Fencing\",\n  \"space\": \"architecture-and-standards\",\n  \"author\": \"Aisha Patel\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-02-15\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-03-01\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Diego Martinez\",\n    \"Sara Kim\",\n    \"Liam O'Connor\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"adr\",\n    \"contract-testing\",\n    \"schema-fencing\",\n    \"ci-cd\",\n    \"conformance\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"/architecture-and-standards/api-standards/canonical-request-schema-and-validation-playbook-2025\",\n    \"/architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/variant-compatibility-ledger-and-stewardship-protocol-2026\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"content\": \"Summary\\n\\nThis ADR defines a company-wide standard for declarative contract tests and a complementary \\\"schema fencing\\\" discipline to prevent schema drift between services and the Redwood platform (APIs, telemetry, and model-serving payloads). The goal is to make API and model I/O contracts machine-testable, versioned, and CI-gated, minimizing production surprises and simplifying rollback and compatibility reasoning.\\n\\nContext and motivation\\n\\nRecent incidents and near-misses were traced to silent schema changes that allowed malformed or unexpectedly shaped requests/telemetry to flow into the runtime. Ad-hoc unit tests are insufficient for cross-service contract guarantees because:\\n\\n- Contracts span teams (edge proxies, gateways, runtime, and client SDKs).\\n- Behavioral compatibility is not captured by type checks alone (e.g., field deprecation with semantic changes).\\n- Runtime routing fallback and model-variant compatibility require an explicit, testable matrix.\\n\\nThis ADR proposes:\\n\\n1. A declarative, YAML-first contract-test spec that lives next to service code and in a central conformance repo for cross-service scopes.\\n2. A \\\"schema fencing\\\" lifecycle that fences allowed shape changes via explicit change proposals, automated conformance checks, and CI gates.\\n3. A conformance status ledger and telemetry for contract drift and failed-matrix cell SLI.\\n\\nScope\\n\\nApplies to:\\n\\n- Public and internal HTTP/GRPC REST endpoints (edge, control-plane, telemetry ingestion).\\n- Model-serving input/output schemas (prompts, structured responses, embeddings metadata).\\n- Streaming/session protocols where message schemas are negotiated.\\n\\nOut of scope:\\n\\n- Internal-only helper functions that are never consumed by other services.\\n- Ad-hoc developer prototypes until they are promoted to a supported service.\\n\\nKey concepts\\n\\nDeclarative contract test spec (DCTS):\\n- A human-friendly YAML format that describes request/response shapes, example inputs, success/failure predicates, and conformance categories (strict, tolerant, deprecated).\\n- DCTS entries can be unit-run (local), CI-run (service-level), and cross-service-run (integration conformance matrix).\\n\\nSchema fencing:\\n- Every change to a DCTS schema field must be accompanied by a Change Proposal (CP) file and an automated compatibility check.\\n- CPs are accepted automatically if they pass compatibility rules or fail open for manual review if they are breaking.\\n\\nConformance matrix and ledger:\\n- A centrally aggregated matrix that tracks which service versions (and model variants) satisfy which DCTS cells.\\n- Each matrix cell has a pass/fail history and a conformance SLI aggregated daily.\\n\\nRules and compatibility classes\\n\\nFields are labeled with one of: required, optional, deprecated, extension. Compatibility rules:\\n\\n- required -> optional: allowed but requires explicit CP and CI signal.\\n- optional -> required: breaking change; requires canary/rollout plan and staged opt-in.\\n- remove deprecated field: allowed only after 3 release cycles and >95% conformance across callers.\\n- add new field marked extension: always allowed if receivers ignore unknown fields (tolerant mode).\\n\\nChange proposal workflow (brief)\\n\\n1. Author creates a CP file in the service repo under docs/contracts/cps/<pr>.yaml describing intent, compatibility class, rollout plan, and rollback criteria.\\n2. CI runs: unit tests, DCTS local run, contract linters, and cross-service dry-run against the latest conformance snapshot.\\n3. If auto-check passes (non-breaking or safe extension), merge proceeds. If flagged as potentially breaking, the CP moves to manual review by contract stewards and product owners.\\n4. After merge, integration conformance jobs run nightly to validate callers and receivers.\\n\\nExample DCTS snippet (YAML)\\n\\n# Example: /v1/generate request/response\\n# Save as service/docs/contracts/dcts/generate.v1.yaml\\n---\\nendpoint: POST /v1/generate\\nscope: public\\nversion: 1.0.0\\nmode: strict\\nrequest: \\n  content-type: application/json\\n  schema: |\\n    type: object\\n    properties:\\n      prompt:\\n        type: string\\n      features:\\n        type: object\\n        additionalProperties: true\\n    required: [prompt]\\nexamples:\\n  - name: simplest\\n    request: {\\\"prompt\\\": \\\"Summarize the following text...\\\"}\\nresponse:\\n  schema: |\\n    type: object\\n    properties:\\n      id: {type: string}\\n      output: {type: string}\\n      tokens_consumed: {type: integer}\\n    required: [id, output]\\npredicates:\\n  - description: output must be non-empty\\n    jq: \\\".output | length > 0\\\"\\nconformance_category: strict\\n\\nAutomation and CI integration\\n\\nCI responsibilities (service repo):\\n- Run local DCTS validation (schema validity, example conformance).\\n- Run contract linter: enforces required metadata fields (owner, risk_level, test_coverage_min).\\n- Publish DCTS artifact to conformance-bucket/<service>/<version>/dcts.yaml on successful merge.\\n\\nCross-repo conformance job (central):\\n- Nightly job that pulls the published DCTS artifacts and runs pairwise checks across known callers and receivers.\\n- Failing cells create RFC-style issues in the responsible service repo and update the conformance ledger with failure signals.\\n\\nConformance ledger and dashboard\\n\\nThe ledger is a time-series-friendly table with columns described below and exposed in the Redwood Console and an internal dashboard. Store as rows in our metrics DB and index in the conformance service. (Table described in prose below.)\\n\\nRequired columns (ledger row): timestamp, service_a, service_a_version, service_b, service_b_version, endpoint, dcts_version, test_case_id, result (pass|fail), failure_reason, run_id.\\n\\nOperational SLOs and alerting\\n\\n- Nightly conformance pass rate for critical public endpoints >= 99.0%. Alert if < 98.0% over a 24-hour rolling window.\\n- Any new CP that causes a regression in an existing passing matrix cell triggers a P1 review if the affected client is production and >= 10% traffic.\\n\\nGating and release policy\\n\\n- Service merge gating: Non-breaking CPs are mergeable. Breaking CPs require manual approval and a staged rollout with canary conformance verifying client behavior.\\n- Platform releases (runtime, SDKs): must maintain 100% conformance for official SDK bindings across supported minor versions.\\n\\nRollout and rollback playbook (high level)\\n\\n1. Pre-merge: author runs smoke DCTS locally and creates CP with rollout notes.\\n2. Merge: DCTS published and cross-repo nightlies scheduled.\\n3. Canary: route 5% traffic to new service variant for 2 hours while conformance checks run.\\n4. Monitor: observe ledger and user-facing errors for regressions.\\n5. If failure SLI breached or critical callers fail, execute rollback to previous version and open an incident review.\\n\\nTelemetry and observability requirements\\n\\nEach contract-test run must emit:\\n- conftest.run_id (UUID)\\n- conftest.service (service name/version)\\n- conftest.endpoint\\n- conftest.test_case_id\\n- conftest.result (pass|fail)\\n- conftest.duration_ms\\n\\nThese fields are sent to the conformance-ingest pipeline with low-cardinality sampling for historical debugging. Link failures to trace IDs when available.\\n\\nOwner and stewardship\\n\\n- Contract steward role: a cross-functional team (API Platform + SRE + Product) that maintains the conformance harness, linter rules, and central ledger.\\n- Service owners: must author and maintain DCTS files for each public surface and model variant.\\n\\nOpen questions and tradeoffs\\n\\n- How strict should default mode be for internal endpoints? Proposal: internal endpoints default to tolerant mode, but any endpoint used by another service must be promoted to strict with a DCTS.\\n- Cost vs. coverage: nightly full-matrix checks are expensive. We propose prioritized sweeps (critical endpoints every night, others weekly).\\n\\nMigration plan\\n\\n1. Pilot: Onboard three services (edge-proxy, runtime-controller, and the embeddings-ingest) to the DCTS and CP workflow over Q2 2026.\\n2. Expand to all public endpoints and model-serving inputs by Q4 2026.\\n3. Enforce gate for new public endpoints starting Q1 2027.\\n\\nAppendix: sample CLI commands and linter config\\n\\n# Local validation\\n#   conftest validate service/docs/contracts/dcts/*.yaml\\n\\n# Publish artifact (CI step)\\n#   conftest publish --bucket=conformance-bucket --service=$SERVICE --version=$VERSION dcts.yaml\\n\\n# Central conformance run (dry-run example)\\n#   conformance-runner --matrix-file=matrix.json --artifacts-dir=artifacts/ --output=ledger.csv\\n\\n# Linter rules (excerpt)\\n# required: [owner, risk_level, conformance_category, test_coverage_min]\\n\\nNotes on documentation style\\n\\n- Keep DCTS files short and example-driven. Prefer real-world examples over exhaustive machine-generated schemas.\\n- Use the CP description field to capture rationale and expected client impact.\\n\\nReferences\\n\\n- See canonical request schema and validation playbook: /architecture-and-standards/api-standards/canonical-request-schema-and-validation-playbook-2025\\n- Variant compatibility ledger: /architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/variant-compatibility-ledger-and-stewardship-protocol-2026\\n\\nApproval\\n\\nApproved by: API Platform leadership, SRE management, and Product for runtime conformance.\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_04b24bf957c047f4b7d8ceefdfde8290\"\n}",

document.content:
{
  "title": "ADR: Declarative Contract Tests and Schema Fencing",
  "space": "architecture-and-standards",
  "author": "Aisha Patel",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-02-15",
  "last_updated": "2026-03-01",
  "reviewers": [
    "Diego Martinez",
    "Sara Kim",
    "Liam O'Connor"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "adr",
    "contract-testing",
    "schema-fencing",
    "ci-cd",
    "conformance"
  ],
  "related_pages": [
    "/architecture-and-standards/api-standards/canonical-request-schema-and-validation-playbook-2025",
    "/architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/variant-compatibility-ledger-and-stewardship-protocol-2026"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "content": "Summary

This ADR defines a company-wide standard for declarative contract tests and a complementary "schema fencing" discipline to prevent schema drift between services and the Redwood platform (APIs, telemetry, and model-serving payloads). The goal is to make API and model I/O contracts machine-testable, versioned, and CI-gated, minimizing production surprises and simplifying rollback and compatibility reasoning.

Context and motivation

Recent incidents and near-misses were traced to silent schema changes that allowed malformed or unexpectedly shaped requests/telemetry to flow into the runtime. Ad-hoc unit tests are insufficient for cross-service contract guarantees because:

- Contracts span teams (edge proxies, gateways, runtime, and client SDKs).
- Behavioral compatibility is not captured by type checks alone (e.g., field deprecation with semantic changes).
- Runtime routing fallback and model-variant compatibility require an explicit, testable matrix.

This ADR proposes:

1. A declarative, YAML-first contract-test spec that lives next to service code and in a central conformance repo for cross-service scopes.
2. A "schema fencing" lifecycle that fences allowed shape changes via explicit change proposals, automated conformance checks, and CI gates.
3. A conformance status ledger and telemetry for contract drift and failed-matrix cell SLI.

Scope

Applies to:

- Public and internal HTTP/GRPC REST endpoints (edge, control-plane, telemetry ingestion).
- Model-serving input/output schemas (prompts, structured responses, embeddings metadata).
- Streaming/session protocols where message schemas are negotiated.

Out of scope:

- Internal-only helper functions that are never consumed by other services.
- Ad-hoc developer prototypes until they are promoted to a supported service.

Key concepts

Declarative contract test spec (DCTS):
- A human-friendly YAML format that describes request/response shapes, example inputs, success/failure predicates, and conformance categories (strict, tolerant, deprecated).
- DCTS entries can be unit-run (local), CI-run (service-level), and cross-service-run (integration conformance matrix).

Schema fencing:
- Every change to a DCTS schema field must be accompanied by a Change Proposal (CP) file and an automated compatibility check.
- CPs are accepted automatically if they pass compatibility rules or fail open for manual review if they are breaking.

Conformance matrix and ledger:
- A centrally aggregated matrix that tracks which service versions (and model variants) satisfy which DCTS cells.
- Each matrix cell has a pass/fail history and a conformance SLI aggregated daily.

Rules and compatibility classes

Fields are labeled with one of: required, optional, deprecated, extension. Compatibility rules:

- required -> optional: allowed but requires explicit CP and CI signal.
- optional -> required: breaking change; requires canary/rollout plan and staged opt-in.
- remove deprecated field: allowed only after 3 release cycles and >95% conformance across callers.
- add new field marked extension: always allowed if receivers ignore unknown fields (tolerant mode).

Change proposal workflow (brief)

1. Author creates a CP file in the service repo under docs/contracts/cps/<pr>.yaml describing intent, compatibility class, rollout plan, and rollback criteria.
2. CI runs: unit tests, DCTS local run, contract linters, and cross-service dry-run against the latest conformance snapshot.
3. If auto-check passes (non-breaking or safe extension), merge proceeds. If flagged as potentially breaking, the CP moves to manual review by contract stewards and product owners.
4. After merge, integration conformance jobs run nightly to validate callers and receivers.

Example DCTS snippet (YAML)

# Example: /v1/generate request/response
# Save as service/docs/contracts/dcts/generate.v1.yaml
---
endpoint: POST /v1/generate
scope: public
version: 1.0.0
mode: strict
request: 
  content-type: application/json
  schema: |
    type: object
    properties:
      prompt:
        type: string
      features:
        type: object
        additionalProperties: true
    required: [prompt]
examples:
  - name: simplest
    request: {"prompt": "Summarize the following text..."}
response:
  schema: |
    type: object
    properties:
      id: {type: string}
      output: {type: string}
      tokens_consumed: {type: integer}
    required: [id, output]
predicates:
  - description: output must be non-empty
    jq: ".output | length > 0"
conformance_category: strict

Automation and CI integration

CI responsibilities (service repo):
- Run local DCTS validation (schema validity, example conformance).
- Run contract linter: enforces required metadata fields (owner, risk_level, test_coverage_min).
- Publish DCTS artifact to conformance-bucket/<service>/<version>/dcts.yaml on successful merge.

Cross-repo conformance job (central):
- Nightly job that pulls the published DCTS artifacts and runs pairwise checks across known callers and receivers.
- Failing cells create RFC-style issues in the responsible service repo and update the conformance ledger with failure signals.

Conformance ledger and dashboard

The ledger is a time-series-friendly table with columns described below and exposed in the Redwood Console and an internal dashboard. Store as rows in our metrics DB and index in the conformance service. (Table described in prose below.)

Required columns (ledger row): timestamp, service_a, service_a_version, service_b, service_b_version, endpoint, dcts_version, test_case_id, result (pass|fail), failure_reason, run_id.

Operational SLOs and alerting

- Nightly conformance pass rate for critical public endpoints >= 99.0%. Alert if < 98.0% over a 24-hour rolling window.
- Any new CP that causes a regression in an existing passing matrix cell triggers a P1 review if the affected client is production and >= 10% traffic.

Gating and release policy

- Service merge gating: Non-breaking CPs are mergeable. Breaking CPs require manual approval and a staged rollout with canary conformance verifying client behavior.
- Platform releases (runtime, SDKs): must maintain 100% conformance for official SDK bindings across supported minor versions.

Rollout and rollback playbook (high level)

1. Pre-merge: author runs smoke DCTS locally and creates CP with rollout notes.
2. Merge: DCTS published and cross-repo nightlies scheduled.
3. Canary: route 5% traffic to new service variant for 2 hours while conformance checks run.
4. Monitor: observe ledger and user-facing errors for regressions.
5. If failure SLI breached or critical callers fail, execute rollback to previous version and open an incident review.

Telemetry and observability requirements

Each contract-test run must emit:
- conftest.run_id (UUID)
- conftest.service (service name/version)
- conftest.endpoint
- conftest.test_case_id
- conftest.result (pass|fail)
- conftest.duration_ms

These fields are sent to the conformance-ingest pipeline with low-cardinality sampling for historical debugging. Link failures to trace IDs when available.

Owner and stewardship

- Contract steward role: a cross-functional team (API Platform + SRE + Product) that maintains the conformance harness, linter rules, and central ledger.
- Service owners: must author and maintain DCTS files for each public surface and model variant.

Open questions and tradeoffs

- How strict should default mode be for internal endpoints? Proposal: internal endpoints default to tolerant mode, but any endpoint used by another service must be promoted to strict with a DCTS.
- Cost vs. coverage: nightly full-matrix checks are expensive. We propose prioritized sweeps (critical endpoints every night, others weekly).

Migration plan

1. Pilot: Onboard three services (edge-proxy, runtime-controller, and the embeddings-ingest) to the DCTS and CP workflow over Q2 2026.
2. Expand to all public endpoints and model-serving inputs by Q4 2026.
3. Enforce gate for new public endpoints starting Q1 2027.

Appendix: sample CLI commands and linter config

# Local validation
#   conftest validate service/docs/contracts/dcts/*.yaml

# Publish artifact (CI step)
#   conftest publish --bucket=conformance-bucket --service=$SERVICE --version=$VERSION dcts.yaml

# Central conformance run (dry-run example)
#   conformance-runner --matrix-file=matrix.json --artifacts-dir=artifacts/ --output=ledger.csv

# Linter rules (excerpt)
# required: [owner, risk_level, conformance_category, test_coverage_min]

Notes on documentation style

- Keep DCTS files short and example-driven. Prefer real-world examples over exhaustive machine-generated schemas.
- Use the CP description field to capture rationale and expected client impact.

References

- See canonical request schema and validation playbook: /architecture-and-standards/api-standards/canonical-request-schema-and-validation-playbook-2025
- Variant compatibility ledger: /architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/variant-compatibility-ledger-and-stewardship-protocol-2026

Approval

Approved by: API Platform leadership, SRE management, and Product for runtime conformance.

    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/linear",
    "content": "{\n  \"key\": \"ENG-12876\",\n  \"team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"title\": \"stabilization-window-rc-eligibility-orchestrator\",\n  \"status\": \"In Progress\",\n  \"priority\": \"P1\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-03-01\",\n  \"updated_at\": \"2026-03-10\",\n  \"creator\": \"Aisha Patel\",\n  \"assignee\": \"Marco Ruiz\",\n  \"project\": \"release-train-2026\",\n  \"cycle\": \"2026-W09\",\n  \"estimate\": \"8\",\n  \"due_date\": \"2026-03-15\",\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"release-engineering\",\n    \"rc-automation\",\n    \"lts\",\n    \"observability\"\n  ],\n  \"dependencies\": [\n    \"ENG-31247\",\n    \"ENG-52391\"\n  ],\n  \"release\": \"runtime-1.22\",\n  \"customer_impact\": \"medium\",\n  \"security_review_required\": \"false\",\n  \"description\": \"Problem: Our current weekly build -> RC tagging flow relies on ad-hoc human checks and a separate release notes generation step. This causes two recurring issues: 1) borderline builds get promoted without a predictable stability gate, increasing hotfix churn on LTS lanes; 2) release notes are assembled manually from PR templates and often miss runtime-impacting changes (batching, KV cache, kernel selection) unless authors explicitly tag them.\\n\\nGoal: Implement a stabilization-window + RC eligibility orchestrator that programmatically evaluates candidate weekly builds across signal tiers (test flakes, canary SLO deltas, perf regressions, eval quality checks) and produces: (a) an explicit RC candidate list with provenance and confidence score; (b) automated RC tagging in git for eligible candidates; (c) automated release notes draft enriched with runtime-impact metadata and links to performance dashboards. The orchestrator should also expose a small human review UI in Console to approve/override candidates before final tagging for the weekly LTS lane.\\n\\nHigh level proposal:\\n- Stabilization window: run a deterministic 48-hour window after each weekly build where the orchestrator aggregates signals and computes an \\\"eligibility_score\\\" per build. Signals include flaky test score (30%), canary SLO delta (30%), per-token latency regression (20%), eval-suite regression rate (15%), and security policy scans (5%).\\n- RC eligibility rules engine: translate score + hard gates into an outcome: eligible/conditional/blocked. Hard gates: critical test failures, policy scan failures, or >2% canary SLO regression => blocked. Conditional builds require human review.\\n- RC tagging automation: for eligible builds, create a lightweight release branch and annotate with metadata (build id, score, signal links), then tag git as rc-{semver}-{date}. If conditional, mark in Console and create a reviewer assignment.\\n- Release notes automation: use PR metadata, label heuristics, and runtime changelog parsers (scan commit messages for keys like BATCHING, KV_CACHE, KERNEL) to synthesize a structured notes draft. Enrich with links to: perf dashboard (grafana), integration test run (CI URL), and eval diff (s3 path). Also include a human-editable summary in Console.\\n\\nNon-goals: full replacement of human judgment for exceptional releases; automatic LTS promotion without explicit approval.\\n\\nTrade-offs considered:\\n- Strict numeric gating vs. fuzzy scoring: chosen hybrid (score + hard gates) to balance automation with engineer oversight.\\n- Time window length: 48h is a compromise between fast weekly cadence and collecting meaningful stability signals. Can be tuned via config.\\n- Complexity of release-note NLP: initial implementation will be rule-based heuristics to keep scope small; later iterations may add ML-based grouping.\\n\\nOperational notes:\\n- The orchestrator will run as a daily job in the release namespace and listen for new weekly build events.\\n- All decisions are recorded in a release provenance log with links to artifacts for audit.\\n- Console feature flags will gate auto-tagging and the human-review UI so we can do staged rollout to internal teams first.\",\n  \"acceptance_criteria\": [\n    \"Orchestrator aggregates signals and computes eligibility score for a weekly build within 1 hour of window close\",\n    \"Eligible builds are auto-tagged with RC tags in main git repository when auto-tagging feature flag is enabled\",\n    \"Conditional builds surface in Console with reviewer assignment and a concise provenance panel\",\n    \"Release notes draft is generated for every candidate and includes links to perf dashboard, CI run, and eval diff\",\n    \"All decisions are logged and queryable via the release provenance dashboard\"\n  ],\n  \"tasks\": [\n    \"Design eligibility scoring formula and threshold defaults (owner: Marco)\",\n    \"Implement signal adapters: flaky test score (CI), canary SLO delta (telemetry), perf regression extractor (perf infra)\",\n    \"Build rules engine and mapping to eligible/conditional/blocked outcomes\",\n    \"Implement git tagging flow + metadata annotation service\",\n    \"Create release-notes synthesizer with PR label and commit tag heuristics\",\n    \"Console: small review UI and feature flag for auto-tagging\",\n    \"Add audit log entries to provenance store and wire to existing release dashboard\",\n    \"End-to-end QA run on internal staging with three weekly builds\"\n  ],\n  \"notes\": [\n    \"Per discussion with PM (Lina Chen) we must include explicit canary SLO delta links so on-call can trace regressions quickly\",\n    \"Initial score weights were tuned after running the formula over the last 12 weeks of historical builds; see spreadsheet in Confluence\",\n    \"We plan to gate auto-tagging behind 'release.auto_tag' feature flag and enable only for non-LTS lanes initially\",\n    \"Ops request: include an 'escape hatch' playbook that allows immediate manual un-tag + emergency hotfix flow\",\n    \"Security scanning adapter will surface policy failures but not block RC tagging until we complete remediation workflow (follow-up ticket)\"\n  ],\n  \"links\": [\n    \"Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/RELEASE/pages/RC+Eligibility+Orchestrator\",\n    \"Design doc draft: https://drive.redwood.com/drive/folders/rc-eligibility-design\",\n    \"Perf dashboard (example): https://grafana.redwood.com/d/perf/weekly-builds?orgId=1\",\n    \"CI flaky score job: https://ci.redwood.com/jobs/flaky-score\",\n    \"GitHub PR for prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/release-tooling/pull/412\",\n    \"Release provenance dashboard: https://console.redwood.com/releases/provenance\"\n  ],\n  \"comments\": [\n    \"2026-03-02 Marco Ruiz: Initial spike completed. Scored last 12 weekly builds locally \\u2014 score correlates with post-release hotfix count (r=0.68). Moving to adapters implementation.\",\n    \"2026-03-04 Priya Singh (QA): Ran E2E on two historical candidates; conditional outcomes appear in Console UI mock. Need better callouts for perf regression magnitude (absolute vs relative).\",\n    \"2026-03-06 Jonah Park (SRE): Concern: auto-tagging could cause noisy tags if canary telemetry lags. Proposal: require telemetry freshness check before tagging. Marcus will add freshness check to the adapter.\",\n    \"2026-03-08 Lina Chen (PM): Approved prioritization for weekly cadence lane. Requested that LTS promotion remain manual for now and that release notes include runtime upgrade impact section.\",\n    \"2026-03-10 Marco Ruiz: Implemented metadata annotation on git tags and wired provenance log. Opening PR for rules engine; feedback requested from SRE and PM on hard gate thresholds.\"\n  ],\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"description\",\n    \"acceptance_criteria\",\n    \"tasks\",\n    \"notes\",\n    \"comments\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_6c5c574ffa31475a965aacd0948f00e2\"\n}",

document.content:
{
  "key": "ENG-12876",
  "team": "engineering",
  "title": "stabilization-window-rc-eligibility-orchestrator",
  "status": "In Progress",
  "priority": "P1",
  "created_at": "2026-03-01",
  "updated_at": "2026-03-10",
  "creator": "Aisha Patel",
  "assignee": "Marco Ruiz",
  "project": "release-train-2026",
  "cycle": "2026-W09",
  "estimate": "8",
  "due_date": "2026-03-15",
  "labels": [
    "release-engineering",
    "rc-automation",
    "lts",
    "observability"
  ],
  "dependencies": [
    "ENG-31247",
    "ENG-52391"
  ],
  "release": "runtime-1.22",
  "customer_impact": "medium",
  "security_review_required": "false",
  "description": "Problem: Our current weekly build -> RC tagging flow relies on ad-hoc human checks and a separate release notes generation step. This causes two recurring issues: 1) borderline builds get promoted without a predictable stability gate, increasing hotfix churn on LTS lanes; 2) release notes are assembled manually from PR templates and often miss runtime-impacting changes (batching, KV cache, kernel selection) unless authors explicitly tag them.\n\nGoal: Implement a stabilization-window + RC eligibility orchestrator that programmatically evaluates candidate weekly builds across signal tiers (test flakes, canary SLO deltas, perf regressions, eval quality checks) and produces: (a) an explicit RC candidate list with provenance and confidence score; (b) automated RC tagging in git for eligible candidates; (c) automated release notes draft enriched with runtime-impact metadata and links to performance dashboards. The orchestrator should also expose a small human review UI in Console to approve/override candidates before final tagging for the weekly LTS lane.\n\nHigh level proposal:\n- Stabilization window: run a deterministic 48-hour window after each weekly build where the orchestrator aggregates signals and computes an \"eligibility_score\" per build. Signals include flaky test score (30%), canary SLO delta (30%), per-token latency regression (20%), eval-suite regression rate (15%), and security policy scans (5%).\n- RC eligibility rules engine: translate score + hard gates into an outcome: eligible/conditional/blocked. Hard gates: critical test failures, policy scan failures, or >2% canary SLO regression => blocked. Conditional builds require human review.\n- RC tagging automation: for eligible builds, create a lightweight release branch and annotate with metadata (build id, score, signal links), then tag git as rc-{semver}-{date}. If conditional, mark in Console and create a reviewer assignment.\n- Release notes automation: use PR metadata, label heuristics, and runtime changelog parsers (scan commit messages for keys like BATCHING, KV_CACHE, KERNEL) to synthesize a structured notes draft. Enrich with links to: perf dashboard (grafana), integration test run (CI URL), and eval diff (s3 path). Also include a human-editable summary in Console.\n\nNon-goals: full replacement of human judgment for exceptional releases; automatic LTS promotion without explicit approval.\n\nTrade-offs considered:\n- Strict numeric gating vs. fuzzy scoring: chosen hybrid (score + hard gates) to balance automation with engineer oversight.\n- Time window length: 48h is a compromise between fast weekly cadence and collecting meaningful stability signals. Can be tuned via config.\n- Complexity of release-note NLP: initial implementation will be rule-based heuristics to keep scope small; later iterations may add ML-based grouping.\n\nOperational notes:\n- The orchestrator will run as a daily job in the release namespace and listen for new weekly build events.\n- All decisions are recorded in a release provenance log with links to artifacts for audit.\n- Console feature flags will gate auto-tagging and the human-review UI so we can do staged rollout to internal teams first.",
  "acceptance_criteria": [
    "Orchestrator aggregates signals and computes eligibility score for a weekly build within 1 hour of window close",
    "Eligible builds are auto-tagged with RC tags in main git repository when auto-tagging feature flag is enabled",
    "Conditional builds surface in Console with reviewer assignment and a concise provenance panel",
    "Release notes draft is generated for every candidate and includes links to perf dashboard, CI run, and eval diff",
    "All decisions are logged and queryable via the release provenance dashboard"
  ],
  "tasks": [
    "Design eligibility scoring formula and threshold defaults (owner: Marco)",
    "Implement signal adapters: flaky test score (CI), canary SLO delta (telemetry), perf regression extractor (perf infra)",
    "Build rules engine and mapping to eligible/conditional/blocked outcomes",
    "Implement git tagging flow + metadata annotation service",
    "Create release-notes synthesizer with PR label and commit tag heuristics",
    "Console: small review UI and feature flag for auto-tagging",
    "Add audit log entries to provenance store and wire to existing release dashboard",
    "End-to-end QA run on internal staging with three weekly builds"
  ],
  "notes": [
    "Per discussion with PM (Lina Chen) we must include explicit canary SLO delta links so on-call can trace regressions quickly",
    "Initial score weights were tuned after running the formula over the last 12 weeks of historical builds; see spreadsheet in Confluence",
    "We plan to gate auto-tagging behind 'release.auto_tag' feature flag and enable only for non-LTS lanes initially",
    "Ops request: include an 'escape hatch' playbook that allows immediate manual un-tag + emergency hotfix flow",
    "Security scanning adapter will surface policy failures but not block RC tagging until we complete remediation workflow (follow-up ticket)"
  ],
  "links": [
    "Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/RELEASE/pages/RC+Eligibility+Orchestrator",
    "Design doc draft: https://drive.redwood.com/drive/folders/rc-eligibility-design",
    "Perf dashboard (example): https://grafana.redwood.com/d/perf/weekly-builds?orgId=1",
    "CI flaky score job: https://ci.redwood.com/jobs/flaky-score",
    "GitHub PR for prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/release-tooling/pull/412",
    "Release provenance dashboard: https://console.redwood.com/releases/provenance"
  ],
  "comments": [
    "2026-03-02 Marco Ruiz: Initial spike completed. Scored last 12 weekly builds locally \u2014 score correlates with post-release hotfix count (r=0.68). Moving to adapters implementation.",
    "2026-03-04 Priya Singh (QA): Ran E2E on two historical candidates; conditional outcomes appear in Console UI mock. Need better callouts for perf regression magnitude (absolute vs relative).",
    "2026-03-06 Jonah Park (SRE): Concern: auto-tagging could cause noisy tags if canary telemetry lags. Proposal: require telemetry freshness check before tagging. Marcus will add freshness check to the adapter.",
    "2026-03-08 Lina Chen (PM): Approved prioritization for weekly cadence lane. Requested that LTS promotion remain manual for now and that release notes include runtime upgrade impact section.",
    "2026-03-10 Marco Ruiz: Implemented metadata annotation on git tags and wired provenance log. Opening PR for rules engine; feedback requested from SRE and PM on hard gate thresholds."
  ],
  "title_field_name": "title",
  "content_field_names": [
    "description",
    "acceptance_criteria",
    "tasks",
    "notes",
    "comments"
  ],
  "dataset_doc_uuid": "dsid_6c5c574ffa31475a965aacd0948f00e2"
}

Priya, can you give a 2-3 minute background\\u2014recent roles, what you've been shipping, and why you're interested in Redwood?\\n[00:32] Priya Rao: Sure. I most recently was at InfraAnalytics where I was a senior solutions engineer supporting AI infra customers, mostly focused on model serving and cost optimizations. I worked a lot with GPU provisioning, autoscaling policies, and helping customers design fallback routing for multi-model setups. I'm excited about Redwood because of the focus on production-grade inference\\u2014I've seen a lot of customers struggle with predictable latency and cost, so the product fit seems good for my background.\\n[01:05] Evan Liu: When you say autoscaling policies, can you give an example\\u2014like what metrics you tuned and tradeoffs you considered?\\n[01:12] Priya Rao: We tuned on queue length and P95 latency for the endpoint. The tradeoff was throughput vs. cold-starts; we had to pick batch windows carefully so spikes didn't blow up latency, and we used a small warm pool to avoid tail latency for critical routes. Also we used quantized weights at night for cost savings on non-critical workloads.\\n[01:38] Sophie Martinez: Nice, that aligns with what our Optimize team talks about. Quick question about customer conversations\\u2014how did you surface reliability concerns without scaring customers about cost?\\n[01:50] Priya Rao: I led with SLOs and a simple example: show them current costs and what latency looks like with and without aggressive batching. I often propose a two-stage rollout: first optimize for cost in staging, then pin to a more conservative config in prod and monitor.\\n[02:10] Evan Liu: Ok, let's do a short troubleshooting scenario. Imagine a customer reports intermittent 5xxs from streaming API when traffic spikes. Walk me through your investigation and immediate mitigations.\\n[02:22] Priya Rao: First I'd confirm the scope: is it a single model, region, or route? Check the gateway and per-route logs, look at KV cache hit rates, and check GPU memory pressure. Immediate mitigations: enable rate-limiting/queue throttling, fallback to a lower-capacity model variant, or divert non-critical traffic to a cached response. For long-term fix, tune batching thresholds and increase warm pool or adjust autoscaler cooldowns.\\n[03:05] Evan Liu: In practice, when you say divert to cached response, what kind of cache policies did you use?\\n[03:12] Priya Rao: Mostly prefix and user-session cache for deterministic flows, TTL-based for semistochastic outputs. We were careful with PII\\u2014consistent with KMS policies\\u2014so cache keys were hashed and encrypted.\\n[03:30] Sophie Martinez: There's sometimes confusion between caching and reranking\\u2014good answer. Follow-up: have you ever helped design a private deployment or VPC/on-prem setup?\\n[03:40] Priya Rao: Yes, we ran a couple private deployments. Main issues were networking: TLS cert management, DNS, and ensuring audit logs to the customer's SIEM. For onboarding we provided runbooks for firewall rules and IAM roles.\\n[03:58] Evan Liu: Any experience with HSM/KMS integrations?\\n[04:02] Priya Rao: Yes, customers usually had a preferred KMS. We wrote examples for AWS KMS and a generic HSM handshake.\\n[04:12] Leah Kim: Priya, quick note on timeline\\u2014are you available for a take-home exercise this week?\\n[04:18] Priya Rao: Yes, I am. I can take it and return within 48 hours.\\n[04:22] Sophie Martinez: Great. Final part: do you have any questions for us?\\n[04:26] Priya Rao: A couple. One, how do teams at Redwood balance latency SLOs vs. model cost when running mixed workloads? Two, what's the typical ramp for a new hire in SE?\\n[04:36] Evan Liu: For the first\\u2014it's a combination of RBAC-based routing and workload tagging; we use profiling to recommend quantization, autoscale settings, and sometimes model-variant routing. {
  "meeting_id": "ff-20250211-001",
  "recorded_at": "2025-02-11T16:00:00-08:00",
  "duration_minutes": "40",
  "call_type": "other",
  "title": "Candidate Interview: Senior Sales Engineer",
  "redwood_owner": "Sophie Martinez",
  "redwood_attendees": [
    "Sophie Martinez",
    "Evan Liu"
  ],
  "customer_company": "Candidate: Priya Rao",
  "customer_attendees": [
    "Priya Rao (Candidate)",
    "Leah Kim (Recruiter)"
  ],
  "transcription_quality": "medium",
  "summary": "First-stage technical interview for a Senior Sales Engineer candidate. Covered candidate background, systems experience, brief product walkthrough, and a short troubleshooting scenario. Agreed on next steps: a take-home assignment and scheduling a panel interview.",
  "topics": [
    "background and experience",
    "technical troubleshooting scenario",
    "Redwood product fit",
    "next steps and scheduling"
  ],
  "next_steps": [
    "Sophie to send take-home assignment by 2025-02-12",
    "Schedule panel interview with PM and Eng by 2025-02-18",
    "Recruiter to confirm candidate availability"
  ],
  "action_items": [
    "Sophie Martinez - send assignment - 2025-02-12",
    "Evan Liu - prepare technical rubric and notes - 2025-02-14",
    "Leah Kim - confirm panel availability - 2025-02-13"
  ],
  "competitors_mentioned": [
    "Databricks",
    "Anthropic"
  ],
  "transcript": "Meeting Header:\nDate: 2025-02-11\nTime: 16:00 PST\nDuration: 40 minutes\nAttendees: Sophie Martinez (Redwood AE), Evan Liu (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Candidate), Leah Kim (Recruiter)\n\n[00:00] Sophie Martinez: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. This is Sophie from Redwood, Evan's with me. Priya, thanks for taking the time today. Can you hear us ok?\n[00:08] Priya Rao: Yes, I can hear you. Thanks for having me.\n[00:12] Evan Liu: Great, we'll start with a quick intro then jump to a short technical scenario. Sounds good?\n[00:16] Priya Rao: Sounds perfect.\n[00:20] Sophie Martinez: Cool. Priya, can you give a 2-3 minute background\u2014recent roles, what you've been shipping, and why you're interested in Redwood?\n[00:32] Priya Rao: Sure. I most recently was at InfraAnalytics where I was a senior solutions engineer supporting AI infra customers, mostly focused on model serving and cost optimizations. I worked a lot with GPU provisioning, autoscaling policies, and helping customers design fallback routing for multi-model setups. I'm excited about Redwood because of the focus on production-grade inference\u2014I've seen a lot of customers struggle with predictable latency and cost, so the product fit seems good for my background.\n[01:05] Evan Liu: When you say autoscaling policies, can you give an example\u2014like what metrics you tuned and tradeoffs you considered?\n[01:12] Priya Rao: We tuned on queue length and P95 latency for the endpoint. The tradeoff was throughput vs. cold-starts; we had to pick batch windows carefully so spikes didn't blow up latency, and we used a small warm pool to avoid tail latency for critical routes. Also we used quantized weights at night for cost savings on non-critical workloads.\n[01:38] Sophie Martinez: Nice, that aligns with what our Optimize team talks about. Quick question about customer conversations\u2014how did you surface reliability concerns without scaring customers about cost?\n[01:50] Priya Rao: I led with SLOs and a simple example: show them current costs and what latency looks like with and without aggressive batching. I often propose a two-stage rollout: first optimize for cost in staging, then pin to a more conservative config in prod and monitor.\n[02:10] Evan Liu: Ok, let's do a short troubleshooting scenario. Imagine a customer reports intermittent 5xxs from streaming API when traffic spikes. Walk me through your investigation and immediate mitigations.\n[02:22] Priya Rao: First I'd confirm the scope: is it a single model, region, or route? Check the gateway and per-route logs, look at KV cache hit rates, and check GPU memory pressure. Immediate mitigations: enable rate-limiting/queue throttling, fallback to a lower-capacity model variant, or divert non-critical traffic to a cached response. For long-term fix, tune batching thresholds and increase warm pool or adjust autoscaler cooldowns.\n[03:05] Evan Liu: In practice, when you say divert to cached response, what kind of cache policies did you use?\n[03:12] Priya Rao: Mostly prefix and user-session cache for deterministic flows, TTL-based for semistochastic outputs. We were careful with PII\u2014consistent with KMS policies\u2014so cache keys were hashed and encrypted.\n[03:30] Sophie Martinez: There's sometimes confusion between caching and reranking\u2014good answer. Follow-up: have you ever helped design a private deployment or VPC/on-prem setup?\n[03:40] Priya Rao: Yes, we ran a couple private deployments. Main issues were networking: TLS cert management, DNS, and ensuring audit logs to the customer's SIEM. For onboarding we provided runbooks for firewall rules and IAM roles.\n[03:58] Evan Liu: Any experience with HSM/KMS integrations?\n[04:02] Priya Rao: Yes, customers usually had a preferred KMS. We wrote examples for AWS KMS and a generic HSM handshake.\n[04:12] Leah Kim: Priya, quick note on timeline\u2014are you available for a take-home exercise this week?\n[04:18] Priya Rao: Yes, I am. I can take it and return within 48 hours.\n[04:22] Sophie Martinez: Great. Final part: do you have any questions for us?\n[04:26] Priya Rao: A couple. One, how do teams at Redwood balance latency SLOs vs. model cost when running mixed workloads? Two, what's the typical ramp for a new hire in SE?\n[04:36] Evan Liu: For the first\u2014it's a combination of RBAC-based routing and workload tagging; we use profiling to recommend quantization, autoscale settings, and sometimes model-variant routing. In product it's a lot of labelling routes by criticality and setting different batch windows.\n[04:52] Sophie Martinez: On ramp\u2014two weeks onboarding then shadowing calls for about a month; you pair with an AE/SE for the first quarter on new accounts.\n[05:00] Priya Rao: That sounds good.\n[05:03] Sophie Martinez: Ok we'll wrap. Leah, we'll send the take-home and schedule the panel. Priya, thanks again.\n[05:10] Leah Kim: Thanks, everyone.\n\n(Transcription notes: occasional overlap and filler words; some technical terms auto-corrected\u2014e.g., KV cache was sometimes transcribed as \"K-V cash\").",

  "content_field_names": [
    "summary",
    "transcript"
  ],

reviewed SSO steps, audit log exposure and retention windows; agreed on SOC2 docs to share; scheduled benchmarks and test windows. A few items flagged for follow-up: SAML metadata, retention matrix, KV cache benchmark.\\n\\nTranscript:\\n[00:00] Samir (Redwood): Hi everyone, thanks for joining on a Friday. quick agenda \\u2014 security handoff, we wanna cover SSO SAML, audit logs retention, and any SOC Two evidence requests. anyone on from Nexora wants to add?\\n[00:12] Lena (Nexora): yeah thanks, uh, quick one, we wanted to make sure the pilot telemetry that you expose is sufficient for compliance, and then second we wanna lock in the retention windows for PII.\\n[00:22] Jules (Redwood): great, i can walk through the audit log surface \\u2014 there are event streams for request headers, model selection, token counts, and redact flags. logs are available through the console or delivered to your S3-like bucket, and we can route them to your SIEM.\\n[00:36] Markus (Nexora): when you say redact flags, is that server-side PII redaction or client-side markers? we need that clarified for audit.\\n[00:44] Jules (Redwood): good call \\u2014 currently we provide markers (meta) and we also have an optional server-side PII scrubber that we can enable in pilot. it's rule-based today, config lives in the private deployment layer, but for hosted pilots we can enable a pre-send filter. it's not perfect, sometimes names slip, so we advise a combination of client-side tokenization + our filter.\\n[01:10] Priya (Nexora): ok and do those logs include full prompts? we can't keep raw prompts beyond our retention window.\\n[01:18] Jules (Redwood): logs capture prompt hash and truncated context by default. full-prompt capture is opt-in and we can deliver it encrypted with K M S integration, or avoid storing it entirely. for the pilot we recommended storing only hashes + truncated context to meet minimal audit needs.\\n[01:36] Samir (Redwood): Markus, from a security architect perspective what's the hill you need us to clear to be comfortable?\\n[01:44] Markus (Nexora): two things \\u2014 1) SAML SSO: we need IdP metadata exchange and a test window to validate assertion attributes (nameid, email, group). 2) audit logs: we need tamper-evident logs and a retention guarantee for 24 months, with export to our S3 with server-side encryption. also we need evidence that keys are rotated and K M S is used.\\n[02:12] Samir (Redwood): got it. we do support SAML and can provide S P metadata; we also have audit log delivery with SSE and we support key rotation \\u2014 i'll send the SOC2 pack for details on controls.\\n[02:28] Lena (Nexora): what's in that SOC Two pack? is it recent?\\n[02:33] Samir (Redwood): it's SOC 2 Type II, covers the last 12 months; includes control narrative, auditor report, and list of policies. i'll bundle it with a retention matrix that outlines where logs live and encryption at rest / transit.\\n[02:46] Priya (Nexora): sweet. on the performance side i want to align the bench \\u2014 Jules you were going to run KV cache / burst tests to ensure latency doesn't spike when we hit 40 requests per second.\\n[02:56] Jules (Redwood): yes \\u2014 on our side we'll run a workload that mirrors your 1.5k daily active agent sessions, with bursts to 60 RPS. we'll capture p50/p90/p99, token cost, and CPU/GPU utilization. note: sometimes the K V cache warm-up can cause initial tail latency \\u2014 we can tune the prefix caching TTL and batching to mitigate.\\n[03:20] Lena (Nexora): any gotchas around private vs hosted? we prefer hosted for speed but security may push us to dedicated or private.\\n[03:28] Samir (Redwood): that's the tradeoff \\u2014 hosted gets you fastest onboarding and telemetry hooks, dedicated gives you VLAN/VPC isolation and customer-managed K M S. during pilot we can run hosted with strict retention & IdP integration, then move to dedicated for final.\\n[03:44] Markus (Nexora): we need a plan B if hosted can't meet our keys requirement. what's minimum time to switch to dedicated?\\n[03:52] Jules (Redwood): in our experience, config and capacity pre-provisioning takes 2-3 weeks once contract and sizing are nailed. we can also provide temporary VPN for audits during pilot to review logs in-place.\\n[04:06] [00:04:06] Samir (Redwood): quick note \\u2014 we sometimes see transcription in these calls mix up VPC as V P C or K V cache as \\\"kiv cache\\\" \\u2014 just ignore the transcript, details in the docs.\\n[04:16] Markus (Nexora): ha, yeah those auto-transcripts are always fun.\\n\\n[05:00] Jules (Redwood): tagging some specifics \\u2014 SAML attributes: we expect nameid, mail, groups. we map groups to RBAC roles in the console; we support SCIM for provisioning but not enabled in pilot by default.\\n[05:14] Priya (Nexora): we do want SCIM later \\u2014 do you have an estimated ETA?\\n[05:19] Jules (Redwood): SCIM is available on Dedicated; for hosted pilots we can do manual provisioning, or enable SCIM in beta if necessary \\u2014 need a short scoping call.\\n\\n[08:10] Lena (Nexora): audit log schema \\u2014 can you show an example?\\n[08:17] Jules (Redwood): sure \\u2014 example event: timestamp, request_id, model_id, token_count, prompt_hash, redaction_flag, user_id (anon if requested), and route. payloads are JSON lines. we can watermarked tamper-evidence by signing log batches.\\n[08:40] Markus (Nexora): the signing \\u2014 is the signature proof verifiable? we need to attest integrity if we hand over log batches to auditors.\\n[08:48] Jules (Redwood): yes, we can provide signed bundles with a checksum and public key verification. we'll include instructions in the SOC docs.\\n\\n[12:05] Samir (Redwood): okay, let's talk retention policy \\u2014 Nexora mentioned 24 months for audit logs, but 90 days for full prompts and 365 for derived embeddings? what's your current desired split?\\n[12:18] Priya (Nexora): suggested baseline: full prompts 90 days, logs 24 months, embeddings 1 year, extracted PII fields removed immediately after extraction unless flagged.\\n[12:29] Markus (Nexora): also need the ability to run on-demand deletion requests (subject access) and an API for that.\\n[12:36] Jules (Redwood): we support selective deletions via an API, and in private deployments we can run a deletion job against the persistent stores. hosted pilot also supports on-demand deletion but we may need a ticket depending on retention tier.\\n\\n[16:00] Lena (Nexora): one small compliance question \\u2014 does your audit trail include admin actions in the console (rollouts, model switches)?\\n[16:08] Jules (Redwood): yes, admin activity is logged. we keep a separate admin audit trail which is also exportable and retains actor metadata.\\n\\n[20:00] Priya (Nexora): for the benchmark \\u2014 what inputs do you need from us?\\n[20:06] Jules (Redwood): ideally: representative prompt sets (anonymized), expected RPS profile, desired max latency SLOs, and a list of model variants to exercise. we'll provision a test harness and replay traffic.\\n[20:18] Priya (Nexora): ok we'll upload a sanitized prompt set to the shared drive.\\n\\n[24:00] Samir (Redwood): ops/pricing \\u2014 Markus asked about the cost delta between hosted with retention guarantees vs dedicated. ballpark numbers?\\n[24:12] Samir (Redwood): hosted with extended retention and K M S on our side is roughly +15% on unit cost, dedicated (customer-managed keys and VPC) is larger \\u2014 depends on reserved capacity commitments. we'll follow up with a tailored pricing sheet.\\n[24:28] Markus (Nexora): that's fine, as long as it's predictable for budgeting.\\n\\n[30:00] Jules (Redwood): technical note \\u2014 the KV cache warm-up is important: recommend TTL prewarm for sessions where you expect sustained interactions. also batching parameters: aggressive batching saves cost but increases p50; we can tune per-route.\\n[30:18] Priya (Nexora): can you provide default batching/ttl settings?\\n[30:22] Jules (Redwood): yes i'll share our recommended config (example: batch_window_ms:20, max_batch_tokens:4096, kv_cache_ttl:600s) \\u2014 just examples; we'll run bench to tune.\\n\\n[36:00] Samir (Redwood): security docs deliverable timeline \\u2014 i'll send SOC2 + control narratives by next Wednesday. Jules will push the benchmark spreadsheet by Friday. Markus, can you confirm IdP metadata by Monday?\\n[36:16] Markus (Nexora): Monday works, we need a four hour window Tuesday afternoon for assertion testing.\\n[36:24] Samir (Redwood): noted, we will schedule that test window.\\n\\n[40:00] Lena (Nexora): any blocker on the ability to export logs to our S3 with SSE?\\n[40:06] Jules (Redwood): none, we support S3 export with SSE-C or SSE-S3 and cross-account role. we'll document the required IAM policy.\\n\\n[44:00] Samir (Redwood): quick recap / next steps \\u2014 action items listed in the doc. we'll reconvene on Monday only if needed after the SAML handoff; otherwise next sync is our end-of-week bench review.\\n[44:18] Priya (Nexora): sounds good. thanks everyone.\\n[44:24] Markus (Nexora): thanks.\\n[44:30] Jules (Redwood): thanks all, we'll follow up with the files.\\n\\nEnd of transcript.\\n\\nNotes / Links mentioned: \\n- SOC2 pack (to be sent)\\n- SAML metadata exchange link (to be shared)\\n- Benchmark spreadsheet (to be uploaded by Jules)\\n- Shared drive: https://drive.internal/nexora-pilot (placeholder)\\n\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"transcript\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_eb6e9aeb654646528cb7553a4dbef0e9\"\n}",

document.content:
{
  "meeting_id": "ff-20260910-nexora-01",
  "recorded_at": "2026-09-10T15:30:00Z",
  "duration_minutes": "48",
  "call_type": "poc_checkin",
  "title": "Nexora Pilot Week 4 - Security Handoff & Retention Review",
  "redwood_owner": "Samir Patel",
  "redwood_attendees": [
    "Samir Patel (AE)",
    "Jules Moreno (SE)"
  ],
  "customer_company": "Nexora AI",
  "customer_attendees": [
    "Lena Ortiz (Head of AI Ops)",
    "Markus Rhee (Security Architect)",
    "Priya Desai (Engineering Manager)"
  ],
  "transcription_quality": "medium",
  "competitors_mentioned": [
    "Anthropic",
    "AstraInfer"
  ],
  "next_steps": [
    "Samir to send SOC 2 Type II evidence pack and retention matrix",
    "Jules to run KV cache / burst benchmark and share raw results",
    "Markus to provide SAML IdP metadata and preferred test window",
    "Priya to confirm PII filtering rules and minimum retention period"
  ],
  "action_items": [
    "Samir Patel: Send SOC2 pack + retention matrix - due 2026-09-15",
    "Jules Moreno: Run KV cache + burst benchmark, upload results - due 2026-09-17",
    "Markus Rhee (Nexora): Provide SAML metadata and test account window - due 2026-09-14",
    "Priya Desai (Nexora): Finalize list of sensitive fields and retention SLAs - due 2026-09-16"
  ],
  "crm_deal_id": "NX-2026-09-poc-0043",
  "topics": [
    "SSO / SAML setup",
    "Audit logs and retention",
    "SOC 2 evidence & controls",
    "Data residency and PII filtering",
    "Performance tuning (KV cache, batching)"
  ],
  "transcript": "Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-09-10 15:30 UTC
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Jules (Redwood SE), Lena (Nexora), Markus (Nexora Sec), Priya (Nexora Eng)

Summary: quick handoff from SE to security owner; reviewed SSO steps, audit log exposure and retention windows; agreed on SOC2 docs to share; scheduled benchmarks and test windows. A few items flagged for follow-up: SAML metadata, retention matrix, KV cache benchmark.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir (Redwood): Hi everyone, thanks for joining on a Friday. quick agenda — security handoff, we wanna cover SSO SAML, audit logs retention, and any SOC Two evidence requests. anyone on from Nexora wants to add?
[00:12] Lena (Nexora): yeah thanks, uh, quick one, we wanted to make sure the pilot telemetry that you expose is sufficient for compliance, and then second we wanna lock in the retention windows for PII.
[00:22] Jules (Redwood): great, i can walk through the audit log surface — there are event streams for request headers, model selection, token counts, and redact flags. logs are available through the console or delivered to your S3-like bucket, and we can route them to your SIEM.
[00:36] Markus (Nexora): when you say redact flags, is that server-side PII redaction or client-side markers? we need that clarified for audit.
[00:44] Jules (Redwood): good call — currently we provide markers (meta) and we also have an optional server-side PII scrubber that we can enable in pilot. it's rule-based today, config lives in the private deployment layer, but for hosted pilots we can enable a pre-send filter. it's not perfect, sometimes names slip, so we advise a combination of client-side tokenization + our filter.
[01:10] Priya (Nexora): ok and do those logs include full prompts? we can't keep raw prompts beyond our retention window.
[01:18] Jules (Redwood): logs capture prompt hash and truncated context by default. full-prompt capture is opt-in and we can deliver it encrypted with K M S integration, or avoid storing it entirely. for the pilot we recommended storing only hashes + truncated context to meet minimal audit needs.
[01:36] Samir (Redwood): Markus, from a security architect perspective what's the hill you need us to clear to be comfortable?
[01:44] Markus (Nexora): two things — 1) SAML SSO: we need IdP metadata exchange and a test window to validate assertion attributes (nameid, email, group). 2) audit logs: we need tamper-evident logs and a retention guarantee for 24 months, with export to our S3 with server-side encryption. also we need evidence that keys are rotated and K M S is used.
[02:12] Samir (Redwood): got it. we do support SAML and can provide S P metadata; we also have audit log delivery with SSE and we support key rotation — i'll send the SOC2 pack for details on controls.
[02:28] Lena (Nexora): what's in that SOC Two pack? is it recent?
[02:33] Samir (Redwood): it's SOC 2 Type II, covers the last 12 months; includes control narrative, auditor report, and list of policies. i'll bundle it with a retention matrix that outlines where logs live and encryption at rest / transit.
[02:46] Priya (Nexora): sweet. on the performance side i want to align the bench — Jules you were going to run KV cache / burst tests to ensure latency doesn't spike when we hit 40 requests per second.
[02:56] Jules (Redwood): yes — on our side we'll run a workload that mirrors your 1.5k daily active agent sessions, with bursts to 60 RPS. we'll capture p50/p90/p99, token cost, and CPU/GPU utilization. note: sometimes the K V cache warm-up can cause initial tail latency — we can tune the prefix caching TTL and batching to mitigate.
[03:20] Lena (Nexora): any gotchas around private vs hosted? we prefer hosted for speed but security may push us to dedicated or private.
[03:28] Samir (Redwood): that's the tradeoff — hosted gets you fastest onboarding and telemetry hooks, dedicated gives you VLAN/VPC isolation and customer-managed K M S. during pilot we can run hosted with strict retention & IdP integration, then move to dedicated for final.
[03:44] Markus (Nexora): we need a plan B if hosted can't meet our keys requirement. what's minimum time to switch to dedicated?
[03:52] Jules (Redwood): in our experience, config and capacity pre-provisioning takes 2-3 weeks once contract and sizing are nailed. we can also provide temporary VPN for audits during pilot to review logs in-place.
[04:06] [00:04:06] Samir (Redwood): quick note — we sometimes see transcription in these calls mix up VPC as V P C or K V cache as "kiv cache" — just ignore the transcript, details in the docs.
[04:16] Markus (Nexora): ha, yeah those auto-transcripts are always fun.

[05:00] Jules (Redwood): tagging some specifics — SAML attributes: we expect nameid, mail, groups. we map groups to RBAC roles in the console; we support SCIM for provisioning but not enabled in pilot by default.
[05:14] Priya (Nexora): we do want SCIM later — do you have an estimated ETA?
[05:19] Jules (Redwood): SCIM is available on Dedicated; for hosted pilots we can do manual provisioning, or enable SCIM in beta if necessary — need a short scoping call.

[08:10] Lena (Nexora): audit log schema — can you show an example?
[08:17] Jules (Redwood): sure — example event: timestamp, request_id, model_id, token_count, prompt_hash, redaction_flag, user_id (anon if requested), and route. payloads are JSON lines. we can watermarked tamper-evidence by signing log batches.
[08:40] Markus (Nexora): the signing — is the signature proof verifiable? we need to attest integrity if we hand over log batches to auditors.
[08:48] Jules (Redwood): yes, we can provide signed bundles with a checksum and public key verification. we'll include instructions in the SOC docs.

[12:05] Samir (Redwood): okay, let's talk retention policy — Nexora mentioned 24 months for audit logs, but 90 days for full prompts and 365 for derived embeddings? what's your current desired split?
[12:18] Priya (Nexora): suggested baseline: full prompts 90 days, logs 24 months, embeddings 1 year, extracted PII fields removed immediately after extraction unless flagged.
[12:29] Markus (Nexora): also need the ability to run on-demand deletion requests (subject access) and an API for that.
[12:36] Jules (Redwood): we support selective deletions via an API, and in private deployments we can run a deletion job against the persistent stores. hosted pilot also supports on-demand deletion but we may need a ticket depending on retention tier.

[16:00] Lena (Nexora): one small compliance question — does your audit trail include admin actions in the console (rollouts, model switches)?
[16:08] Jules (Redwood): yes, admin activity is logged. we keep a separate admin audit trail which is also exportable and retains actor metadata.

[20:00] Priya (Nexora): for the benchmark — what inputs do you need from us?
[20:06] Jules (Redwood): ideally: representative prompt sets (anonymized), expected RPS profile, desired max latency SLOs, and a list of model variants to exercise. we'll provision a test harness and replay traffic.
[20:18] Priya (Nexora): ok we'll upload a sanitized prompt set to the shared drive.

[24:00] Samir (Redwood): ops/pricing — Markus asked about the cost delta between hosted with retention guarantees vs dedicated. ballpark numbers?
[24:12] Samir (Redwood): hosted with extended retention and K M S on our side is roughly +15% on unit cost, dedicated (customer-managed keys and VPC) is larger — depends on reserved capacity commitments. we'll follow up with a tailored pricing sheet.
[24:28] Markus (Nexora): that's fine, as long as it's predictable for budgeting.

[30:00] Jules (Redwood): technical note — the KV cache warm-up is important: recommend TTL prewarm for sessions where you expect sustained interactions. also batching parameters: aggressive batching saves cost but increases p50; we can tune per-route.

{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_59cb294da8964683bb165a3bb615df71",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/jira/ops-requests/INT-460811-edge-switch-arp-proxy-ip-duplication.json",
    "title": "Edge switch ARP proxying leads to VPN client IP duplication and intermittent routing to wrong host",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/jira",
    "content": "{\n  \"key\": \"INT-460811\",\n  \"project\": \"internal-support\",\n  \"issue_type\": \"Incident\",\n  \"summary\": \"Edge switch ARP proxying leads to VPN client IP duplication and intermittent routing to wrong host\",\n  \"status\": \"In Progress\",\n  \"priority\": \"P2\",\n  \"severity\": \"Sev2\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-03-10\",\n  \"updated_at\": \"2026-03-14\",\n  \"reporter\": \"Aisha Malik\",\n  \"assignee\": \"Jonah Reed\",\n  \"components\": [\n    \"edge-network\",\n    \"vpn\",\n    \"dhcp\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"networking\",\n    \"arp-proxy\",\n    \"investigation\",\n    \"high-impact\"\n  ],\n  \"environment\": \"prod-us-west\",\n  \"linked_issues\": [\n    \"INT-424246\",\n    \"INT-542019\"\n  ],\n  \"description\": \"Issue summary: Several users reporting intermittent loss of access to internal services while connected to corporate VPN. Symptoms include duplicate IP conflict alerts on endpoints, frequent VPN re-auth events, and traffic appearing to be routed to a different on-prem host (service 10.23.5.12). Impact: ~8% of VPN sessions in us-west over the last 48h experienced short blackholes (30-90s) impacting git pushes, internal CI jobs, and ssh sessions. Scope: affects users on Wi-Fi SSID 'Redwood-Corp' behind specific edge switches in building SF2 rack 7.\",\n  \"steps_to_reproduce\": [\n    \"1) Connect laptop to 'Redwood-Corp' Wi-Fi in SF2 building (tested on macOS 13 and Ubuntu 22.04)\",\n    \"2) Establish VPN session to redwood-vpn-usw.redwood.net (WireGuard-based corporate VPN)\",\n    \"3) Trigger continuous ping to an internal host (ping -i 0.2 10.23.5.12)\",\n    \"4) Observe intermittent duplicate IP warnings on client and packets forwarded to an unexpected MAC on the L2 domain\",\n    \"5) Reproduce frequency increases when there is a short burst of multicast/mDNS traffic on the same AP's radio\"\n  ],\n  \"observed_logs_and_artifacts\": [\n    \"Client syslog excerpt: 'kernel: arp: IP address 10.23.8.45 claimed by 00:11:22:33:44:55 (conflict)'\",\n    \"Switch (edge-sw-7) log: 'proxy-arp conflict detected for 10.23.8.45, source 00:66:77:88:99:AA bridging-port 5'\",\n    \"Packet capture (pcap) snippet: ARP reply for 10.23.8.45 with two different source MACs within 120ms\",\n    \"VPN server metrics: client rekey count spike (client 10.23.8.45) correlated to timestamp 2026-03-12T14:12Z\",\n    \"Internal service (10.23.5.12) reported TCP reset spikes aligning with client blackholes\"\n  ],\n  \"investigation_notes\": [\n    \"Hypothesis 1: Edge switch proxy-arp configured for legacy NAT path is responding to ARP for VPN-assigned addresses from an overlapping DHCP pool, causing two active ARP entries on the LAN.\",\n    \"Hypothesis 2: A misconfigured VXLAN/bridge on edge-sw-7 is advertising ARP for the VPN subnet into the campus L2 segment when multicast bursts occur.\",\n    \"What we tried: - Disabled proxy-arp on edge-sw-7 port-channel to AP group temporarily (no immediate reduction). - Isolated a suspect AP by moving a test client to a different AP (blackhole persisted only when client served by AP-7A). - Captured pcap on AP, switch uplink, and VPN server concurrently for correlated timestamps (pcaps saved to /mnt/logs/INT-460811/pcaps/).\",\n    \"Preliminary find: ARP 'gratuitous' replies with VPN client IP are being injected by the switch's 'proxy-arp' feature only when the AP's multicast queue exceeds threshold. The switch returns ARP for the same IP with a different MAC that matches a spare management interface in rack 7 (00:66:77:88:99:AA).\"\n  ],\n  \"impact_summary\": \"Intermittent connectivity loss for internal developer workflows (git/ssh/CI). Approximately 8% of VPN sessions in the SF2 us-west site affected in the window; potential for data-transfer retries and CI flakiness. No customer-facing outage but notable developer productivity hit.\",\n  \"initial_triage_actions\": [\n    \"1) Placed affected edge switch (edge-sw-7) in monitoring schedule and enabled debug logging for proxy-arp events.\",\n    \"2) Temporarily increased DHCP lease affinity for VPN pool for clients in SF2 to reduce the window for IP reuse.\",\n    \"3) Asked campus networking team to disable 'proxy-arp' global feature on a staging switch and observe (ongoing).\",\n    \"4) Notified platform reliability and CI owners of potential re-run needs for impacted jobs (Slack #incidents and #platform-alerts).\"\n  ],\n  \"comments\": [\n    \"2026-03-11 09:18 - Jonah Reed: Assigned to network; will coordinate switch config changes and gather pcaps. Next action: schedule maintenance window if we need to push config rollback.\",\n    \"2026-03-12 15:25 - Priya Shah (campus-net): Reproduced proxy-arp responses on edge-sw-7 when AP multicast queue > 70%. Suspect firmware 1.2.3 on these switches has a known misc bridging bug. Opened ticket with vendor (TAC-889233).\",\n    \"2026-03-13 08:52 - Jonah Reed: Vendor TAC confirmed the switch may respond to ARP for non-local subnets under multicast overload in 1.2.3. Recommended immediate mitigation: set 'proxy-arp disable' on VRF for AP VLANs and upgrade firmware to 1.2.6.\",\n    \"2026-03-14 07:30 - Aisha Malik: Applied 'proxy-arp disable' to edge-sw-7 in staged maintenance window (07:00-07:15). Monitoring: VPN rekey spikes reduced from 47/hr to 2/hr for affected clients in the first 24h.\",\n    \"2026-03-14 10:02 - Jonah Reed: Confirming RFC and rollout plan for global fix. Proposed follow-up: firmware upgrade across SF2 rack 4-9, audit for proxy-arp enabled on other edge switches, and update config baseline to explicitly disable proxy-arp for VPN/DHCP subnets.\"\n  ],\n  \"root_cause\": \"Switch firmware (1.2.3) bug caused proxy-arp behavior under high multicast load leading to ARP advertisements for VPN-assigned addresses. This created ephemeral duplicate IP assignments on the L2 domain and caused VPN clients to experience routing blackholes and rekeys.\",\n  \"resolution_notes\": [\n    \"Mitigation applied: 'proxy-arp disable' set on edge-sw-7 AP VLANs during maintenance window 2026-03-14 07:00-07:15.\",\n    \"Temporary workaround: increased DHCP lease affinity and moved high-multicast APs to separate RF profile to reduce multicast bursts.\",\n    \"Permanent fix: planned firmware upgrade to 1.2.6 across SF2 edge switches (racks 4-9) and config baseline change to disable proxy-arp for VPN/DHCP subnets. Vendor TAC provided patch notes and recommended upgrade path.\",\n    \"Follow-ups: - Create change request CR-2026-0415 for firmware rollout. - Run campus-wide audit script to detect 'proxy-arp' enabled instances and remediate. - Add regression test to onboarding checklist for AP multicast stress.\",\n    \"Status: Partial fix applied and validated; full remediation scheduled (see CR-2026-0415).\"\n  ],\n  \"related_github_prs\": [\n    \"https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-config/pull/411\"\n  ],\n  \"related_confluence_pages\": [\n    \"https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/NET/pages/Edge+Switch+Proxy-ARP+Runbook\"\n  ],\n  \"original_location\": \"jira/internal-support/INT-460811-edge-switch-arp-proxy-ip-duplication.json\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"summary\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"description\",\n    \"steps_to_reproduce\",\n    \"observed_logs_and_artifacts\",\n    \"investigation_notes\",\n    \"impact_summary\",\n    \"initial_triage_actions\",\n    \"comments\",\n    \"root_cause\",\n    \"resolution_notes\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_59cb294da8964683bb165a3bb615df71\"\n}",

document.title: Edge switch ARP proxying leads to VPN client IP duplication and intermittent routing to wrong host
document.content:
{
  "key": "INT-460811",
  "project": "internal-support",
  "issue_type": "Incident",
  "summary": "Edge switch ARP proxying leads to VPN client IP duplication and intermittent routing to wrong host",
  "status": "In Progress",
  "priority": "P2",
  "severity": "Sev2",
  "created_at": "2026-03-10",
  "updated_at": "2026-03-14",
  "reporter": "Aisha Malik",
  "assignee": "Jonah Reed",
  "components": [
    "edge-network",
    "vpn",
    "dhcp"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "networking",
    "arp-proxy",
    "investigation",
    "high-impact"
  ],
  "environment": "prod-us-west",
  "linked_issues": [
    "INT-424246",
    "INT-542019"
  ],
  "description": "Issue summary: Several users reporting intermittent loss of access to internal services while connected to corporate VPN. Symptoms include duplicate IP conflict alerts on endpoints, frequent VPN re-auth events, and traffic appearing to be routed to a different on-prem host (service 10.23.5.12). Impact: ~8% of VPN sessions in us-west over the last 48h experienced short blackholes (30-90s) impacting git pushes, internal CI jobs, and ssh sessions.
